claim: Haghani and White (Elm Wealth, 2024-12-05): MSTR common equity about 2.4x the roughly $40B of bitcoin it owns; they expect the premium to shrink over time ("surprised if MSTR is not at a discount in five years") but would not short MSTR against BTC ("We hate being short with unlimited downside ... the likelihood of getting squeezed out seems especially high") and would not buy a 1x long-BTC/short-MSTR ETF.
quote: We hate being short with unlimited downside, and in this case, the likelihood of getting squeezed out seems especially high.
limitations: Practitioner blog, no backtest of a rules-based spread; opinion on tail risk of the short leg; written at premium 2.4x, before the 2025-26 compression.
impact_on_spec: Motivates reporting the short-DAT-only side separately and stressing borrow (3% and 15% per year); the symmetric side is the control.

claim: Lee, Shleifer and Thaler (JF 1991, NBER w3465): closed-end fund discounts are driven by individual investor sentiment, move together, and narrow when small stocks do well.
quote: fluctuations in discounts on closed end funds are driven by changes in individual investor sentiment
limitations: Closed-end funds 1960s-1980s, not crypto treasuries; discount variation is a sentiment-plus-arbitrage-cost story, not proof of a tradeable reversion after 10 bp costs.
impact_on_spec: Prior that premium/discount to holdings mean-reverts but slowly (reason for a 20-session horizon and 120/250 windows).

claim: Pontiff (QJE 1996): closed-end fund deviations from asset value are larger for hard-to-replicate portfolios, low-dividend funds, small funds and when interest rates are high; arbitrage costs allow large price deviations.
quote: Arbitrage costs lead to large deviations of prices from fundamentals.
limitations: Abstract page only (full text restricted); 1990s closed-end funds.
impact_on_spec: Costs and short-selling frictions explain why a premium may persist; supports treating the short-DAT leg with borrow stress.
